experiment.title: SPTAN1 SH3 domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the SPTAN1 SH3 domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the SH3 domain in SPTAN1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P07751_PF00018_968.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Storkhead-box protein, winged-helix domain in STOX1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q6ZVD7_PF10264_112.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Zinc finger, CCCH-type domain in TOE1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q96GM8_PF00642_298.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the B-box-type zinc finger domain in TRIM36 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q9NQ86_PF00643_208.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.title: UBE2K Ubiquitin-associated domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the UBE2K Ubiquitin-associated domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Ubiquitin-associated domain in UBE2K using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P61086_PF00627_158.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

scoreSets.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the VAV1 SH3 domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: VAV1 SH3 domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the VAV1 SH3 domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the SH3 domain in VAV1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P15498_PF00018_592.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

experiment.title: WNK1 Serine/threonine-protein kinase OSR1/WNK, CCT domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the WNK1 Serine/threonine-protein kinase OSR1/WNK, CCT domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Serine/threonine-protein kinase OSR1/WNK, CCT domain in WNK1 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is Q9H4A3_PF12202_481.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the ZBTB24 Zinc finger C2H2-type domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Zinc finger C2H2-type domain in ZBTB24 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is O43167_PF00096_435.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.

scoreSets.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the ZFP36 Zinc finger, CCCH-type domain from domainome 1.0.

experiment.title: ZFP36 Zinc finger, CCCH-type domain from domainome 1.0
experiment.shortDescription: Stability measurements of the ZFP36 Zinc finger, CCCH-type domain from domainome 1.0.
experiment.abstractText: This study measured the stability of the Zinc finger, CCCH-type domain in ZFP36 using a DHFR protein-fragment complementation assay that couples the cellular abundance of the target protein expressed in yeast to yeast growth. The identifier used in the original study is P26651_PF00642_105.
experiment.methodText: Oligonucleotide libraries encoding the domains were generated using mMPS synthesis technology (BGI). Variant domain sequences were fused to a fragment of an essential gene (DHFR) and transformed into yeast cells. Unstable domains are degraded by the cell, reducing DHFR fragment concentration and impeding cell growth in the presence of methotrexate. A total of 27 selections (3 replicates each of 9 sub-libraries) were performed. Variant frequencies before and after cell growth were measured by high-throughput sequencing of amplicon libraries containing the mutated domains. Fitness associated with each variant and their errors were derived using DiMSum v1.2.11 (Faure et al., 2020).

primaryPublicationIdentifiers.title: Site saturation mutagenesis of 500 human protein domains reveals the contribution of protein destabilization to genetic disease
primaryPublicationIdentifiers.abstract: Missense variants that change the amino acid sequences of proteins cause one third of human genetic diseases1. Tens of millions of missense variants exist in the current human population, with the vast majority having unknown functional consequences. Here we present the first large-scale experimental analysis of human missense variants across many different proteins. Using DNA synthesis and cellular selection experiments we quantify the impact of >500,000 variants on the abundance of >500 human protein domains. This dataset - Human Domainome 1.0 - reveals that >60% of pathogenic missense variants reduce protein stability. The contribution of stability to protein fitness varies across proteins and diseases, and is particularly important in recessive disorders. We show how stability measurements can be combined with protein language models to annotate functional sites and that measurements made on a small number of proteins can be used to accurately predict stability changes across entire protein families using energy models. Domainome 1.0 demonstrates the feasibility of assaying human protein variants at scale and provides a large consistent reference dataset for clinical variant interpretation and the training and benchmarking of computational methods.
